newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition supporters march in rain.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition supporters march in rain.

text.p: Tens of thousands of protesters marched through Belgrade on Tuesday keeping up pressure on Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic to concede defeat in local elections.
Serbian opposition leaders said their protests against annulment of November 17 elections were gaining momentum.
Opposition supporters marched in pouring rain through the capital Belgrade, hurling abuse at the state television station -- a symbol of Milosevic's authoritarian rule.
The demonstrators, including children and pensioners, pelted the building with eggs and some threw stones, shattering several windows on the ground floor.
Authorities have brought in hundreds of police with riot gear but so far officers have kept a low-profile and the protests have remained peaceful.

The Zajedno (Together) coalition has led Serbia's biggest demonstrations in five years after accusing authorities of stealing their victory in run-off local elections. Zajedno says the ruling Socialist party made a mockery of democracy by annulling the results due to unspecified irregularities.
An opposition demonstration in Belgrade drew an estimated 150,000 on Monday in a mounting confrontation which Zajedno leaders said amounted to a "democratic revolution".
Not since 1991 have so many taken to the streets against Milosevic.
Protests were under way in other towns and several thousand people attended an opposition rally in the neighbouring republic of Montenegro, independent Belgrade radio B-92 reported.
Earlier, some 10,000 students from Belgrade university staged a march at midday, chanting against Milosevic.
"There are no lessons in Belgrade today," one professor told the students. "This is a lesson -- a lesson in democracy."
Joined by at least 30 law professors, students halted traffic as they marched past foreign embassies and ministries.
They hurled eggs and a few stones at offices of the Yugoslav United Left, the party led by Milosevic's Marxist wife. The students said they planned sit-ins at five faculties.
The United States has condemned the annulment of the municipal election results, which had shown victories for the Zajedno coalition in 15 of the country's 18 biggest towns.

Charges that authorities committed massive fraud prompted the European Union on Monday to postpone giving the Yugoslav republics of Serbia and Montenegro preferential trade status granted to other countries in the region.
Zoran Djindjic, who has emerged as the dominant opposition figure, told Reuters on Monday the opposition protests would soon turn into a campaign of civil disobedience.

"In the end, we will call the people to resort to other methods, to strikes in factories and schools. I think everything is going according to plan." But it was still unclear if the opposition could mobilise workers to strike.

Electoral commissions and courts last week annulled poll results in almost all towns where Zajedno claimed victory. In Belgrade, a court on Sunday stripped Zajedno of a majority in the city council which authorities earlier confirmed.
Electoral commissions have called for another round of voting on Wednesday and Sunday.
Zajedno has urged a boycott of the third round in the capital. Opposition leaders in some towns said they would run in the third round despite their objections.
